Field surveys conducted in the coastal waters of the Arabian Gulf have provided detailed reproductive metrics for the Blackspot snapper Lutjanus ehrenbergii. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from reproductively active females collected during the peak spawning season revealed a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 1.2% [GSI = 1.2%] at the prevailing water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. This modest index is consistent with the pattern of multiple batch spawning observed in many lutjanid species, where individual spawning events are spaced over an extended reproductive period rather than representing a single massive allocation of resources to a single clutch. The eggs produced are small and pelagic, with an average diameter of 0.85 mm. At a water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], the wet weight at birth was calculated to be 0.00032 g [Wwb = 0.00032 g], a value that places the neonates among the smallest of the genus and suggests a strategy reliant on high fecundity to offset the high mortality risks associated with a prolonged planktonic larval phase.

The early ontogeny of Lutjanus ehrenbergii is characterized by a rapid transition from the endotrophic to the exotrophic phase, a period critical for larval survival in oligotrophic tropical waters. Following fertilisation, the yolk-sac larva, or alevin, emerges from the incubating egg through chorion rupture after approximately five days [ab = approximately five days] when held at a stable temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C]. This brief embryonic duration, typical of tropical marine teleosts, minimizes the window of vulnerability for the developing embryo to benthic predators and physical disturbance. Upon hatching, the newly emerged larva, with an initial body mass of just 0.00032 g [Wwb = 0.00032 g], relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for nourishment. The rapid depletion of these yolk stores, coupled with the opening of the mouth and the differentiation of the retina, marks the onset of exogenous feeding, a trophic switch that commits the larva to a planktonic existence where prey availability directly dictates early growth and survival trajectories.

Growth trajectories derived from length-frequency analysis of commercial catches and otolith microstructure studies have established the asymptotic size parameters for this species. The ultimate fork length, representing the theoretical maximum size that individuals can attain, was estimated at 35 cm [Li = 35 cm], a moderate value compared to larger congeners such as Lutjanus sebae. This asymptotic dimension corresponds to a calculated ultimate wet weight of 582 grams [Wwi = 582 grams], a mass that is achieved only by the oldest and most dominant individuals in the population. A critical life-history milestone for female Blackspot snapper is the attainment of puberty, which was determined to occur at a fork length of 20.1 cm [Lp = 20.1 cm]. At this length, the predicted wet weight at puberty is approximately 113.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 113.4 grams], representing a substantial investment in somatic growth before the onset of reproductive activity. This size threshold ensures that females have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the high metabolic demands of vitellogenesis and batch spawning.
